lessons.title: Micro-organisms in meat
lessons.html:
The invisible hazard

Micro-organisms are living things too small to see without a microscope: bacteria, viruses, moulds, yeasts and parasites. Most are harmless, and some are useful, but some cause meat to spoil and others cause disease in people. The meat examiner's job is to help make sure meat leaving the abattoir is safe and wholesome, as required by the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000.

Where contamination comes from

Muscle inside a healthy animal is almost free of bacteria. Contamination happens mainly during slaughter and dressing:

  • Hide, hair and fleece covered in dung and soil.
  • Gut contents if the intestines or stomach are cut or the gullet and rectum are not tied off properly.
  • Hands, knives, gloves and clothing of workers.
  • Equipment and surfaces such as saws, hooks and tables.
  • Water, air, pests such as flies and rodents.

Important bacteria

OrganismNotes
SalmonellaFrom the gut; causes food poisoning
E. coli (including harmful strains such as O157)Faecal contamination; some strains cause severe illness
Listeria monocytogenesGrows even at fridge temperatures; dangerous to pregnant women, babies and the elderly
Staphylococcus aureusFrom skin, nose and infected cuts of workers
Clostridium perfringensSpore former; problems in cooked meat cooled too slowly
CampylobacterCommon in poultry

Conditions for growth

Bacteria need food, moisture, the right temperature and time. Many multiply fastest between about 5 °C and 60 °C, the 'danger zone'. Under good conditions some bacteria can double in number about every 20 minutes. This is why fast chilling of carcasses and keeping the cold chain unbroken are so important.

lessons.title: Meat safety: preventing contamination
lessons.html:
Keeping meat safe from slaughter to dispatch

Principles

  1. Keep micro-organisms off the meat: clean animals, careful dressing, hygienic workers and equipment.
  2. Stop them from growing: chill quickly and keep cold.
  3. Remove or kill them where possible: trimming visible contamination, approved carcass washes or interventions where allowed.

Key hygiene practices on the line

  • Animals should arrive clean and dry. Very dirty animals may need to be held back or handled specially.
  • Skin and open carcasses without letting the outside of the hide touch the meat.
  • Tie or seal the gullet and rectum to stop gut contents leaking.
  • Sterilise knives between carcasses and after any contamination, in hot water at the temperature required by the regulations (commonly at least 82 °C).
  • Wash hands often, and always after touching the hide, gut or floor.
  • Trim visible faecal contamination off; do not just wash it, as washing can spread bacteria.
  • Keep clean and dirty areas separate.

Chilling and the cold chain

Carcasses must go into chillers promptly after dressing. Chillers must not be overloaded and carcasses must hang so that air moves around them. Temperatures are monitored and recorded. Meat is dispatched only when it reaches the required temperature and is transported in clean, refrigerated vehicles.

Zoonoses and residues

Some animal diseases spread to people through meat or handling, such as tuberculosis, cysticercosis (measles) from tapeworm cysts, and brucellosis. Meat inspection detects many of these. Chemical residues from remedies are prevented by farmers following withdrawal periods; abattoirs may sample for residues under official programmes.

HACCP

Abattoirs use Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) systems to identify hazards and control them at critical points, such as chilling temperature or zero visible faecal contamination at final inspection.

lessons.title: Meat quality
lessons.html:
Safe meat that consumers want

Meat quality covers the features that customers value: colour, tenderness, juiciness, flavour, fat cover and shelf life. Quality is influenced on the farm, during transport and lairage, during slaughter and in chilling.

Muscle to meat

After death, muscle runs out of oxygen. Glycogen (stored sugar) in the muscle changes into lactic acid and the pH drops from about neutral to around 5,5 in normal meat. Rigor mortis (stiffening) sets in, then slowly resolves as enzymes tenderise the meat during ageing.

Stress-related quality defects

DefectCauseAppearance
Dark, firm, dry (DFD) or dark cuttingLong-term stress or exhaustion before slaughter uses up glycogen, so pH stays highDark, sticky meat with poor shelf life
Pale, soft, exudative (PSE)Acute stress just before slaughter, mainly in pigs; pH falls too fast while the carcass is still warmPale, watery meat
BruisingRough handling, overcrowding, horns, poor vehiclesDamaged tissue that must be trimmed

Calm handling, enough rest and water in lairage, and correct stunning reduce these problems and support animal welfare under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.

Chilling and quality

Chilling too fast while the meat is still in pre-rigor state can cause 'cold shortening', making meat tough. Abattoirs balance fast chilling for safety with methods that protect tenderness.

Spoilage

Signs include off smells, slime, colour changes and mould. Spoiled meat must not be passed for human consumption.

Key points

  • Most meat contamination comes from hide, gut contents, hands and equipment.
  • Bacteria grow fastest in the danger zone; chill quickly and keep cold.
  • Sterilise knives, wash hands and trim visible contamination.
  • Pre-slaughter stress causes DFD and PSE meat.
  • HACCP controls hazards at critical points.

Hide, gut contents, hands and equipment

quiz.question: Which bacterium can grow even at fridge temperatures?
What should be done with visible faecal contamination on a carcass?

options.text: Wash it off with a hose

quiz.question: Dark cutting (DFD) meat is caused by:

options.text: Long-term stress that uses up muscle glycogen

quiz.question: Why are the gullet and rectum tied off during dressing?

options.text: To prevent gut contents leaking onto the carcass
